title: What a GPU accelerates, and what it cannot make fast
theory: distinguish latency from throughput, independent tasks from dependent chains, and parallelizable work from serial overhead. Start with a concrete image transformation and a sequential running balance. Explain why moving data and launching work are part of the job. Derive a small Amdahl-law example and identify its assumptions.
evidence: a decomposition diagram and a justified decision to accelerate or keep two tasks on CPU.
mistake: more GPU cores imply every program becomes faster.
mechanism: A CPU is optimized to make progress on a comparatively small number of complicated instruction streams. A GPU spends more of its resources on throughput across many pieces of work. This is a design distinction, not a rule that the GPU wins. A dependency means that one result must exist before another calculation can start. Pixel brightness updates have independent destinations; a running account balance has a dependency between successive balances. There can still be a parallel prefix algorithm for that balance, but changing the algorithm is real work. Include loading data, launching kernels and returning results when deciding whether acceleration helps a person waiting for an answer.
example1: Suppose an application spends 20 seconds parsing and 80 seconds transforming pixels. An imagined GPU makes the transform ten times faster and adds 4 seconds of transfers. The new time is \(20 + 8 + 4 = 32\) seconds, so the application speedup is 3.125. The tenfold kernel improvement is not the application improvement. Even an infinitely fast transform leaves 24 seconds under these assumptions.
example2: For one tiny request, suppose CPU arithmetic costs 2 microseconds, while GPU submission and transfers cost 30 microseconds before arithmetic. A 0.2 microsecond kernel gives 30.2 microseconds end to end. Batching 1,000 independent requests may amortize overhead, but it changes waiting time and memory usage. Neither result follows from a core count.
code:
cpu = 20 + 80
gpu = 20 + 80 / 10 + 4
assert gpu == 32
assert cpu / gpu == 3.125
assert 100 / 40 == 2.5
print({"CPU_seconds": cpu, "modeled_GPU_seconds": gpu, "speedup": cpu / gpu})

tasks.question: Construct a 100-second workload with 60 seconds parallelizable and no transfer cost; compute the best possible speedup.
tasks.answer: The 40-second serial part remains. The upper bound is \(\frac{100}{40} = 2.5\), even with an infinitely fast parallel part.

tasks.question: A report compares a 2 ms CPU request against a 0.1 ms kernel and claims 20 times faster. Identify the missing observations.
tasks.answer: Record upload, allocation, launch, synchronization and download costs with the same input and output contract before computing application speedup.

tasks.question: What changes if the input contains zero pixels?
tasks.answer: The mathematical output is empty. A host guard can return immediately instead of launching an empty grid; fixed overhead otherwise dominates.

tasks.question: Would you accelerate a chain of 1,000 dependent HTTP requests using a CUDA kernel?
tasks.answer: CUDA does not remove network waiting or dependency ordering. First change the request architecture or batch independent work; do not infer a compute bottleneck.

title: Meet the hardware without memorizing a product catalog
theory: CPU cores, GPU streaming multiprocessors, warps, arithmetic pipelines, registers, shared memory, caches, device memory, copy engines and host interconnect. Distinguish a programming thread from a physical arithmetic lane and an SM from a CPU core. Introduce compute capability as a feature contract, not the installed toolkit number.
evidence: labeled hardware/software map and a capability report if hardware exists.
mistake: every launched thread occupies its own permanent physical core.
mechanism: An SM, or streaming multiprocessor, schedules groups of GPU threads and owns finite execution and storage resources. A block is a cooperating group in your program; it is not a physical processor. Blocks can wait for resources and need not run in index order. Within a block, threads are organized into warps, normally 32 threads in CUDA. A warp issues instructions with a set of participating lanes. Registers hold per-thread working values, shared memory supports block cooperation, and device DRAM holds larger arrays. Copy engines may transfer data while computation proceeds, but concurrency depends on hardware and dependencies. Compute capability identifies a hardware feature family; toolkit version identifies software.
example1: Draw four SM boxes and a grid of ten blocks. Under the deliberately simplified assumption of one resident block per SM, the grid needs at least three waves: four, four and two blocks. This is an occupancy illustration, not a runtime prediction. Real residency depends on registers, shared memory, threads and architectural limits.
example2: A block with 100 threads occupies four warps. The last warp contains four valid program threads and 28 unused lane positions. A kernel with 100 blocks does not require 10,000 physical arithmetic units. Scheduling reuses execution resources over time. Do not build a dependency that assumes block 0 finishes first.
code:
from math import ceil

assert ceil(10 / 4) == 3
assert [ceil(n / 32) for n in (31, 32, 33, 100)] == [1, 1, 2, 4]
print({"simplified_waves": ceil(10 / 4), "warps_for_100_threads": ceil(100 / 32)})

tasks.question: Calculate the warp count for blocks with 31, 32 and 33 threads.
tasks.answer: Ceiling division by 32 yields one, one and two warps. The second warp in the last case has one program thread.

tasks.question: A program labels its toolkit version as the GPU compute capability. Repair the inventory.
tasks.answer: Record device model and compute capability from device properties separately from compiler/toolkit, driver and framework versions.

tasks.question: Can ten blocks require more than three waves in the four-SM drawing?
tasks.answer: Yes. The drawing ignores resource pressure, uneven duration and scheduling effects; it establishes a simplified lower bound only.

tasks.question: Map a 2 MiB array through host memory, transfer engine, device DRAM and an SM.
tasks.answer: Data starts in host storage, is transferred to device allocation, and loads feed SM registers or shared memory. Returned output needs an explicit or framework-managed dependency and transfer.

title: The software stack from application to driver
theory: host driver, CUDA runtime and driver APIs, toolkit, compiler, user-space libraries, framework packages and container image. Explain what `nvcc`, a framework CUDA build and `nvidia-smi` each tell us, including what none proves alone. Separate the host operating-system boundary from container contents.
evidence: correctly place six failure messages at their responsible layer.
mistake: installing a CUDA Python package or compiler installs a usable NVIDIA GPU.
mechanism: An application calls a runtime API or a higher-level library. User-space CUDA libraries then cooperate with the host NVIDIA driver to access a device. A container packages application code and user-space dependencies; it does not package a physical GPU or replace the host kernel driver. The toolkit includes tools such as the nvcc compiler. A framework wheel may bring compatible CUDA user-space components without a general-purpose CUDA compiler. Conversely, nvcc can exist on a machine where no GPU is visible. Each observation answers a different question: compilation, driver management access, framework device discovery, allocation and numerical execution are separate checks.
example1: A shell reports `nvcc: command not found`, while an already installed framework executes a tensor operation on a GPU. This is possible because the framework can run precompiled kernels without the developer compiler. Building a new CUDA extension has a different dependency contract from running the existing tensor operator.
example2: A container contains nvcc and compiles a program, but `cudaGetDeviceCount` reports no available device. Editing the kernel cannot repair absent hardware access. Inspect host support, driver and deliberate container GPU exposure. The compiler result remains valid compilation evidence; record execution as unavailable instead of silently presenting a CPU result as CUDA success.

tasks.question: Order these layers: kernel driver, application, CUDA runtime, GPU.
tasks.answer: Application calls runtime; runtime uses the kernel driver; the driver controls the GPU. Libraries and framework dispatch can add intermediate layers.

tasks.question: A driver-management command succeeds but an allocation fails. What next?
tasks.answer: Preserve the exact allocation status and requested bytes. Check device visibility, compatibility and available memory rather than treating management visibility as a successful compute test.

tasks.question: What can a CPU-only Mac complete in this chapter?
tasks.answer: The layer diagrams, diagnostic classification and CPU models. A Linux container on that Mac does not create an NVIDIA CUDA device.

tasks.question: Design a capability label for a build-only machine.
tasks.answer: Use 'CUDA compilation available; GPU execution not verified'. Keep hardware, driver access and actual allocation/execution observations separate.

expected_output: Compilation evidence only; no GPU execution evidence.

title: Parallel decomposition before launch syntax
theory: domain decomposition, task decomposition, work, dependency depth, granularity, load balance and boundary work. Introduce map, reduce, scan, gather and scatter as reusable patterns. Distinguish the mathematical operation from its scheduling.
evidence: a decomposition that covers every element once and states synchronization requirements.
mistake: an evenly divisible toy size proves the indexing scheme works generally.
mechanism: Decomposition assigns parts of a problem to workers while preserving its mathematical meaning. A map transforms each input independently. A reduction combines many values into one. A scan produces every prefix, so its outputs encode more information than a reduction. Gather reads from chosen locations; scatter writes to chosen locations and needs a conflict policy when destinations overlap. Work counts all operations, while dependency depth counts the longest chain that cannot be parallelized. A useful decomposition names each output owner, describes required inputs and states when producers must finish before consumers read.
example1: Partition 10 elements into conceptual blocks of four. The ownership ranges are [0,4), [4,8) and [8,10). The half-open notation includes the start and excludes the end. Each element appears once; the final block has a tail. Allocating three full blocks of output without a bounds predicate would incorrectly expose positions 10 and 11.
example2: For \([2,1,3,4]\), reduction returns 10. Inclusive scan returns \([2,3,6,10]\), and exclusive scan returns \([0,2,3,6]\). A reduction alone cannot tell element 2 where to write in a stable filtered output. That position comes from a prefix count of earlier selected elements.
code:
values = [2, 1, 3, 4]
prefix, total = [], 0
for value in values:
    prefix.append(total)
    total += value
assert prefix == [0, 2, 3, 6] and total == 10
ranges = [list(range(start, min(start + 4, 10))) for start in range(0, 10, 4)]
assert sum(ranges, []) == list(range(10))
print({"exclusive_scan": prefix, "reduction": total, "ownership": ranges})

tasks.question: Tile a width-7, height-3 image with conceptual 4-by-2 tiles.
tasks.answer: Four tiles cover it. Predicate both x<7 and y<3; the right and bottom tiles contain invalid lane positions.

tasks.question: Two scatter workers both write output\([2]\). Explain why unique input indices are insufficient.
tasks.answer: Unique readers do not imply unique output ownership. Define an atomic combine, collision-free destination calculation or a staged grouping algorithm.

tasks.question: Give the reduction and scan of an empty vector under integer addition.
tasks.answer: The reduction identity is zero; both scans are empty. An implementation should define these cases before launching work.

tasks.question: Choose map, reduce or scan for allocating stable filtered output positions.
tasks.answer: Map produces selection flags, exclusive scan gives each selected element's destination, and the final prefix plus flag gives output count.

title: Memory as addresses, ownership, shape and stride
theory: bytes versus elements, dtype, alignment, contiguous storage, row-major and column-major layout, strides, views, aliasing and ownership. Distinguish a pointer value from the authority to dereference that address on a particular processor.
evidence: a correct offset table and explicit ownership/lifetime diagram.
mistake: two arrays with the same shape necessarily have the same layout or independent storage.
mechanism: A shape says how many logical coordinates exist. A stride says how far to move in storage when a coordinate increases by one. A row-major two-dimensional float array with row stride s elements places coordinate (r,c) at element offset r*s+c, then multiplies by the element size to obtain a byte offset. Padded rows use s greater than their logical width. A view can change shape and strides while borrowing the same allocation. Copying an address does not extend the allocation's lifetime or create independent data. Device and host pointers also carry an accessibility contract beyond their printed numeric value.
example1: Take a 2-by-3 float32 matrix with five stored elements per row. Coordinate (1,2) has element offset \(1\times 5+2=7\) and byte offset 28. The logical six values occupy a padded allocation of ten floats, or 40 bytes. Multiplying by logical width would read element 5 instead, a different location.
example2: For contiguous \([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]\), the row-major strides are (3,1) elements. A transposed view has shape (3,2) and strides (1,3). Coordinate (2,1) still refers to underlying element 5, value 6. There was no mandatory movement of bytes, and writing through the view can change the original owner.
code:
rows, cols, stride, itemsize = 2, 3, 5, 4
assert ((1 * stride + 2) * itemsize) == 28
storage = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
transposed = [[storage[r + c * 3] for c in range(2)] for r in range(3)]
assert transposed == [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
print({"offset_bytes": 28, "transpose_view_values": transposed})

tasks.question: Compute the byte offset of (2,3) in a padded float64 matrix with row stride 8.
tasks.answer: The element offset is \(2\times 8+3=19\); at eight bytes per element the offset is 152 bytes.

tasks.question: A kernel receives only shape (3,2) for a transposed view and assumes contiguous rows. Diagnose the failure.
tasks.answer: Shape omits the stride contract. Pass actual strides or make and account for a contiguous copy before dispatch.

tasks.question: What changes for a one-column matrix with padding?
tasks.answer: Its column coordinate stays zero, but row steps still use the stored leading dimension. Width one does not imply adjacent row values.

tasks.question: Compare particle position reads in array-of-structures and structure-of-arrays.
tasks.answer: An x-only kernel reads separated x fields in records versus neighboring x values in a dedicated array. Include conversion and other consumers before choosing layout.

title: Numbers, units and a trustworthy answer
theory: finite precision, integer overflow, floating-point reduction order, cancellation, absolute versus relative error, NaN/Inf and problem conditioning. Explain why a tolerance belongs to an algorithm and input range. Use explicit rendered math for reference error and units.
evidence: a testing policy specifying reference precision, tolerance and adversarial cases.
mistake: bitwise CPU/GPU equality is always necessary, or a loose tolerance makes any result acceptable. .
mechanism: Floating-point arithmetic stores a finite approximation to a real number. Adding a small quantity to a large one may round away the small quantity; subtracting similar large values can expose that loss. Relative error scales with a reference magnitude, while absolute error remains meaningful near zero. A common comparison accepts an error no larger than absolute tolerance plus relative tolerance times reference magnitude. The tolerances must come from input ranges, precision and the calculation, not from repeatedly widening them until a broken index passes. Check finite output explicitly, and use exact comparison for integer counts that cannot overflow.
example1: The exact sum of \([10^{16},1,-10^{16}]\) is 1. A sequential binary64 addition can return 0 because \(10^{16}+1\) rounds back to \(10^{16}\). Python's compensated `math.fsum` recovers 1 for this fixture. Different summation order is a numerical mechanism, not proof that either processor is faulty.
example2: Compare output 0.00000004 with reference zero under absolute tolerance 0.0000001. It passes. A relative-only rule with zero reference would reject every nonzero result. Conversely, output 4 where reference is 3 cannot be excused as ordinary small rounding under those tolerances; first investigate shape, indexing and the mathematical contract.
code:
import math

values = [1e16, 1.0, -1e16]
naive = 0.0
for value in values:
    naive += value
assert naive == 0.0 and math.fsum(values) == 1.0
assert abs(4e-8) <= 1e-7
print({"sequential": naive, "compensated_reference": math.fsum(values)})

tasks.question: With \(\mathrm{atol}=0.001\) and \(\mathrm{rtol}=0.01\), find the allowed error at reference 20.
tasks.answer: The bound is \(0.001+0.01\times 20=0.201\). This is a chosen acceptance policy, not a universal CUDA tolerance.

tasks.question: A result contains NaN and a comparison test silently returns false. Repair the test.
tasks.answer: Require finite values before tolerance evaluation and reject NaN or infinity unless the specification explicitly expects them.

tasks.question: Why can signed 32-bit integer accumulation fail despite exact input values?
tasks.answer: The sum can exceed the representable range. Bound the worst-case sum or accumulate using a sufficiently wide type.

tasks.question: Design a histogram oracle.
tasks.answer: Compare every integer bin exactly and verify total count. Include empty, all-in-one-bin and out-of-range input policies; floating tolerance is unnecessary.

title: From elapsed time to a performance model
theory: FLOPs, bytes moved, arithmetic intensity, bandwidth, launch overhead, warm versus cold state, and kernel time versus end-to-end time. Derive a simple roofline bound using clearly hypothetical hardware parameters before showing a captured report. Explain what the bound omits.
evidence: a units-correct model and an experiment that could disprove it.
mistake: peak TFLOPS predicts every kernel, or a kernel speedup is automatically an application speedup.
mechanism: Arithmetic intensity measures operations per byte of data movement under an explicitly stated memory model. A roofline estimate limits performance by the smaller of arithmetic capacity and bandwidth times intensity. It is an upper bound, not a timer. Vector addition reads two float32 values and writes one for one addition, giving roughly one operation per twelve useful bytes before cache and transaction effects. Matrix multiplication can reuse each loaded value many times; tiling increases reuse but consumes working storage. Launch cost, transfer cost, dependency stalls and imperfect access patterns can keep measured work far below either bound.
example1: Assume hypothetical bandwidth of 600 GB/s, using decimal billions, and a 12-byte-per-element vector addition. The ideal useful-element throughput is 50 billion elements/s. One million elements require at least 20 microseconds at that bandwidth, excluding launch and host transfer. This is a thought experiment, not a claim about the learner's GPU.
example2: A hypothetical device has 10 TFLOP/s arithmetic capacity and 500 GB/s bandwidth. At intensity 2 FLOP/byte the roofline is 1 TFLOP/s; at intensity 40 it is capped at 10 TFLOP/s. Increasing reuse can change the limiting resource, but a kernel must still expose sufficient independent work.
code:
n, bytes_per_element, bandwidth = 1_000_000, 12, 600e9
seconds = n * bytes_per_element / bandwidth
assert abs(seconds - 20e-6) < 1e-15
limits = [min(10e12, intensity * 500e9) for intensity in (2, 40)]
assert limits == [1e12, 10e12]
print({"ideal_memory_seconds": seconds, "roofline_flops_per_second": limits})

tasks.question: Estimate useful bytes for adding two length-1,000 float64 vectors.
tasks.answer: Two eight-byte reads and one eight-byte write per element gives 24,000 useful bytes. Measured transactions and cache traffic can differ.

tasks.question: A calculation divides bytes by TFLOP/s and calls the result seconds. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: The units do not cancel. Divide bytes by bytes/s for memory time, or floating operations by operations/s for arithmetic time.

tasks.question: Why is a roofline less useful for a one-element kernel?
tasks.answer: Fixed launch and synchronization overhead dominate; the asymptotic bandwidth model omits that term.

tasks.question: A tiled kernel reduces global reads but doubles register use. What evidence decides?
tasks.answer: Correctness first, then measured time, compiler resource usage and selected memory/occupancy metrics on the same workload. Reduced estimated bytes alone is insufficient.

title: Reproducibility, safety and the first evidence notebook
theory: record input generation, seed, shape, dtype, hardware, software, launch parameters, warm-up, repetitions and timing scope. Separate scientific reproducibility from byte-identical parallel floating-point output. Explain memory budgets and why arbitrary infinite GPU loops are inappropriate on a shared or display device.
evidence: a reusable experiment template and correctly labeled capability status.
mistake: a screenshot of a timing or a driver version is sufficient runtime evidence.
mechanism: A reproducible experiment records enough context to explain why a result happened. An input seed is useful only alongside the generator, dtype, shape and distribution. A benchmark needs timing scope, warm-up policy and retained samples, while a correctness result needs an independent expected answer. Hardware access, successful compilation, successful execution and acceptable numerical output are four distinct observations. A resource budget limits input size and repeated work before running. On a shared GPU, reserve only the memory and compute time that the owner has authorized; do not use unbounded spin loops as teaching fixtures.
example1: Report A says 'GPU: 0.2 ms'. Report B records a synthetic float32 vector of 1,024 elements, seed 7, upload excluded, five warm-ups, twenty event-timed samples, device/toolkit identities and an absolute error bound. B is interpretable, but it still needs raw samples and CPU comparison before supporting a speedup claim.
example2: A vector-add oracle uses \([0,-2,5]\) and \([3,2,-1]\), expecting \([3,0,4]\). Add length-zero and a 33-element fixture to expose assumptions about block boundaries. This reference can run on any CPU. Label it CPU correctness evidence rather than evidence that a GPU kernel has run.
code:
x, y = [0, -2, 5], [3, 2, -1]
assert [a + b for a, b in zip(x, y)] == [3, 0, 4]
assert 3 * 1_000_000 * 4 == 12_000_000
receipt = {"surface": "CPU reference", "shape": [3], "result": [3, 0, 4], "gpu_executed": False}
print(receipt)

tasks.question: Write five required fields for a correctness receipt.
tasks.answer: Source identity, exact bounded input, reference method, observed result or error, and execution environment/capability are a useful minimum.

tasks.question: A run was cancelled but marked passed because the compiler exited zero. Correct the record.
tasks.answer: Compilation passed; execution was cancelled or incomplete. A separate completed numerical comparison is required for runtime acceptance.

tasks.question: How should a no-device run be represented?
tasks.answer: Unavailable or skipped with the actual reason, never a successful CUDA result and never a fabricated timing.

tasks.question: Design a memory budget for three float32 vectors of one million elements.
tasks.answer: Their raw payload is 12 MB total. Add library workspace and runtime overhead separately and reject larger input before allocation.

title: C++ essentials specifically needed at the GPU boundary
theory: fixed-width types, references and pointers, `const`, contiguous containers, `size_t`, conversions, function parameters and compile-time versus runtime values. Keep this a bridge, linking to existing C++ teaching for full language explanations.
evidence: CPU reference tests and a lifetime explanation.
mistake: copying a pointer copies the data, or a host container can be passed to device code unchanged.
mechanism: A pointer identifies storage; a size defines the range your function may use. Pair them explicitly. A const input pointer prevents writes through that pointer, but it does not establish unique ownership or guarantee that another alias cannot modify storage. A vector owns contiguous elements and can lend its data pointer while it remains alive and does not reallocate. A device function cannot generally use an ordinary host vector object because its implementation, allocator and storage belong to the host environment. Use plain element buffers and explicit shape metadata at the boundary, with deliberate integer-width choices for address arithmetic.
example1: A CPU affine transform accepts input, output, count, scale and bias. For input \([-1,0,2]\), scale 3 and bias 1, the result is \([-2,1,7]\). Reject mismatched ranges before indexing. If input and output overlap, either document in-place safety or reject that case; const alone does not answer it.
example2: A function returning `vector<float>{1,2,3}.data()` returns a pointer to storage whose owner is destroyed at the end of the expression. The pointer value may still print, but dereferencing it is invalid. Return the owning vector, or pass caller-owned storage into the function. Keeping a numeric address does not keep an allocation alive.
code:
values = [-1, 0, 2]
result = [3 * value + 1 for value in values]
assert result == [-2, 1, 7]
padded = [1, 2, 99, 3, 4, 99]
row_sums = [sum(padded[r * 3 : r * 3 + 2]) for r in range(2)]
assert row_sums == [3, 7]
print({"affine": result, "row_sums": row_sums})

tasks.question: Describe a row-sum function's minimum buffer metadata for padded storage.
tasks.answer: Input pointer, row count, column count and leading dimension, plus an output buffer and capacity. State element type and accessibility.

tasks.question: A vector grows after its data pointer was saved. What must be checked?
tasks.answer: Growth may reallocate, invalidating borrowed pointers. Reacquire pointers after changes and prevent outstanding consumers from using the old storage.

tasks.question: How should count zero be handled?
tasks.answer: Return without dereferencing either pointer. Do not use an empty range as permission to form invalid pointer arithmetic.

tasks.question: Why should a host pointer not be reinterpreted as a device allocation?
tasks.answer: A cast changes the C++ type, not allocation location, accessibility or ownership. Use a supported memory allocation and transfer contract.

title: Resource ownership and failure-safe cleanup
theory: allocation ownership, move-only handles, destructors, exception boundaries and status-returning APIs. Design a simple device-buffer owner on paper before implementing the real device allocation later. Explain cleanup on a partially completed initialization.
evidence: no double release, no leaked first allocation, and clear owner/borrower relationships.
mistake: adding a destructor alone guarantees correctness when copies are still allowed.
mechanism: RAII connects resource lifetime to an owning C++ object's lifetime. Its constructor establishes an invariant, and its destructor releases the resource. Copying a unique owner is usually forbidden; moving transfers ownership and leaves the source empty. This is important for CUDA allocations, streams and events because a copied raw handle does not represent an independent resource. A destructor should not throw during stack unwinding. Error reporting for explicit completion and release should happen in a deliberate path, while final cleanup remains a last safeguard. Asynchronous use adds a further obligation: do not destroy the owner while a queued operation still borrows the resource.
example1: An operation acquires buffer A, then fails to acquire B. If A already belongs to an automatic owner, stack unwinding releases A. The event trace is acquire-A, acquire-B-failed, release-A. If A is only a raw pointer and cleanup exists only at the normal return, the failure path leaks A.
example2: Moving owner A into owner B changes who releases the allocation. The moved-from A stores an empty handle; only B releases the original resource. A default copy that leaves two nonempty owners would lead to two releases. Neither a destructor nor a smart-sounding class name alone proves this invariant.
code:
events = []
try:
    events.append("acquire-A")
    try:
        events.append("acquire-B-failed")
        raise RuntimeError("synthetic allocation failure")
    finally:
        events.append("release-A")
except RuntimeError:
    pass
assert events == ["acquire-A", "acquire-B-failed", "release-A"]
print(events)

tasks.question: Write the ownership invariant for a device-buffer wrapper.
tasks.answer: Each live nonempty allocation has exactly one owner; borrowers never release it, moves empty the source, and destruction happens after outstanding uses finish.

tasks.question: A destructor throws while handling an earlier allocation exception. Why is this dangerous?
tasks.answer: An exception during unwinding can terminate the process. Keep destructor cleanup nonthrowing and report operational failures through an explicit checked path.

tasks.question: What should an empty owner release?
tasks.answer: Nothing. Represent the empty state distinctly so partial initialization and moved-from objects are safe.

tasks.question: Extend ownership to two streams borrowing one buffer.
tasks.answer: Record both consumers' completion dependencies before freeing or reusing the buffer. Host scope exit alone does not prove GPU completion.

title: The `.cu` file, compiler driver and executable
theory: host and device compilation, `.cu`/`.cuh`, host compiler compatibility, runtime linking, PTX, cubin, fatbinary and just-in-time loading. Show each artifact's purpose. Start with one `main.cu`, a fixed reviewed compile command, visible diagnostics and a clear output executable path.
evidence: preserved compiler output plus a source-to-executable diagram.
mistake: an executable containing device code proves the device can execute it. .
mechanism: A .cu translation unit can contain ordinary host functions and CUDA device functions. nvcc coordinates separate compilation paths, invokes a supported host compiler and links the CUDA runtime. PTX is a virtual instruction representation; a cubin holds device machine code for a target architecture. An executable can package several device images in a fat binary. Loading may select a compatible image or invoke supported JIT compilation of PTX. This explains why source compilation, host linking, device loading and kernel execution can fail at different times. Header suffix .cuh is a convention, not an instruction that executes anything.
example1: The manual lab command is `nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -lineinfo main.cu -o main`. The input is main.cu; `-o main` names the executable. `./main` runs that file from the current directory. The toolkit's default target must support the actual device. A release build later needs deliberately selected architecture targets, not guessed values from a tutorial.
example2: A missing semicolon is a source diagnostic. An undefined host function is a host-link diagnostic. 'No kernel image is available for execution on the device' is a loading/target problem. Replacing arithmetic in the kernel is unlikely to solve the latter. Save the complete diagnostic and identify the stage before changing versions.
code:
stages = ["source", "host/device compilation", "link", "load", "execute", "validate"]
assert stages.index("link") < stages.index("execute")
assert stages.index("execute") < stages.index("validate")
print(" -> ".join(stages))

tasks.question: Distinguish a .cu source file, PTX file and host executable.
tasks.answer: Source is authored C++/CUDA, PTX is virtual device instructions, and the executable contains host code plus packaged device code and link dependencies.

tasks.question: Why is successful nvcc compilation not a GPU test?
tasks.answer: Compilation can happen without a visible GPU. Device loading, allocation, launch and returned-value validation remain separate steps.

tasks.question: What does an executable permission error say about the kernel?
tasks.answer: Nothing yet. The host did not start the program; inspect the exact file path and permissions before GPU diagnosis.

tasks.question: Design a release record for a compiled CUDA binary.
tasks.answer: Record toolkit and host compiler, target architectures/PTX policy, linked library versions, source revision and actual device runtime tests.

expected_output: source -> host/device compilation -> link -> load -> execute -> validate

title: The first bounded kernel and the truth about completion
theory: `__global__`, `__device__`, `__host__`, launch configuration and asynchronous launch. Teach every token in the first example, the distinction between launch failure and execution failure, and explicit completion before reading results or exiting.
evidence: host validates the returned values and reports both launch and completion status.
mistake: returning from the launch expression means the kernel finished. .
mechanism: The `__global__` qualifier declares a kernel callable through CUDA launch syntax. In `fill<<<blocks, threads>>>(out,n)`, the angle-bracket configuration chooses a grid of blocks and threads per block; parentheses carry ordinary function arguments. Each thread reads its own indices to choose work. A launch normally submits work asynchronously. Checking cudaGetLastError after submission detects launch problems, while a checked synchronization or dependent copy exposes execution failures. Only after the dependency is complete should the host validate returned values. Device printf is a debugging tool with ordering and buffering limitations, not a replacement for checking the output buffer.
example1: Let one kernel write its global index into a five-element output using eight launched threads. Threads 0 through 4 write \([0,1,2,3,4]\); threads 5 through 7 perform no write because the bounds predicate is false. The host compares every returned value with its expected index.
example2: Change the expression to twice the index plus one. Expected output is \([1,3,5,7,9]\). Keeping the same ownership mapping separates the arithmetic change from scheduling. A launch status of success without a completion check does not establish these values arrived in host memory.
code:
n, launched = 5, 8
out = [None] * n
for i in range(launched):
    if i < n:
        out[i] = 2 * i + 1
assert out == [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
print({"CPU_ownership_trace": out, "GPU_execution": "not performed"})

tasks.question: Identify the configuration and arguments in fill<<<2,32>>>(out,50).
tasks.answer: Two blocks with 32 threads each are launched, and out plus count 50 are kernel arguments. Fourteen thread positions must avoid writing.

tasks.question: The process exits immediately after submission. What evidence is missing?
tasks.answer: Checked completion, transfer of output and host validation. Successful submission alone does not establish a finished kernel.

tasks.question: What should count zero do?
tasks.answer: Use a host early return or another explicitly valid empty-work policy; do not launch a grid with zero blocks.

tasks.question: Write a useful success message.
tasks.answer: State the actual device, count and validated result contract after completion. Avoid claiming performance or general correctness from five values.

title: Explicit device allocation and transfer
theory: allocation sizes, error checking, host/device memory spaces, transfer directions, buffer lifetimes and zero-length behavior. Introduce deliberate cleanup on every exit without hiding the sequence behind a large helper framework.
evidence: unchanged guard values, correct output, checked statuses and cleanup after an injected host-side failure.
mistake: equal numerical addresses imply interchangeable host and device pointers.
mechanism: cudaMalloc requests a number of bytes and returns a device allocation handle through a pointer argument. For n float elements, calculate n*sizeof(float), checking multiplication bounds for externally supplied sizes. cudaMemcpy also takes bytes and an explicit direction in the simple runtime API. The input owner must remain alive until the transfer finishes, and the device output must remain allocated until its final consumer completes. Host-to-device transfer supplies input; device-to-host transfer produces an observable result. A pointer is not a container with a length field, so the surrounding program must preserve size and lifetime metadata.
example1: Copy \([2,4,6,8]\) as float32. Four elements require 16 bytes. A request for four bytes copies only one float. Zero-initialized test data can hide that error, so use distinct nonzero entries and validate the entire result after the round trip.
example2: Place sentinel values around a three-element target: \([-99,1,2,3,-99]\). Transform only positions 1 through 3 by doubling, expecting \([-99,2,4,6,-99]\). Guards reveal writes beyond the intended subrange, but they do not prove absence of every possible invalid read; sanitizers add a different check.
code:
storage = [-99, 1, 2, 3, -99]
for i in range(1, 4):
    storage[i] *= 2
assert storage == [-99, 2, 4, 6, -99]
assert 4 * 4 == 16 and 33 * 8 == 264
print({"guarded_output": storage, "four_float32_bytes": 16})

tasks.question: How many bytes hold 33 double values?
tasks.answer: \(33\times 8 = 264\) bytes for ordinary eight-byte double representation; use sizeof(double) in actual C++ rather than a copied literal.

tasks.question: A copy uses count where the API expects bytes. Which fixture catches it?
tasks.answer: Distinct nonzero values across the entire range, plus full host comparison. A one-element or all-zero example may conceal the partial copy.

tasks.question: Define an empty-vector transfer policy.
tasks.answer: Return a valid empty result without allocation, copy or kernel launch; never dereference a missing data pointer.

tasks.question: Design cleanup after a failed output allocation.
tasks.answer: Release every earlier owned allocation and preserve the original error. Do not read nonexistent output or report a successful numerical comparison.

title: One-dimensional indexing that survives awkward sizes
theory: global thread index, ceiling division, bounds predicates and grid-stride loops. Derive the coverage proof for the indexing pattern. Explain integer overflow risk in products and use appropriately sized indexing.
evidence: every output element is written exactly once and tails match the CPU reference.
mistake: removing the bounds condition is harmless because a chosen demo length is divisible by the block size.
mechanism: A one-dimensional launch gives a thread the starting index blockIdx.x*blockDim.x+threadIdx.x. A grid-stride loop advances that index by blockDim.x*gridDim.x until it reaches n. Every nonnegative index has one remainder modulo the positive stride, so exactly one starting thread owns it. Cast to a sufficiently wide integer before multiplying dimensions; widening after an overflow is too late. Ceiling division supplies enough threads for one-element mapping, but a grid-stride loop also allows a bounded grid to cover a much larger input. A bounds test is required even when most demonstration sizes divide evenly.
example1: Use two blocks of four threads for \(\mathrm{n}=19\). Thread 0 owns indices 0,8,16; thread 1 owns 1,9,17; thread 2 owns 2,10,18; thread 3 owns 3,11. Every element has exactly one owner. This ownership trace is CPU reasoning, not a simulator of warp scheduling or GPU timing.
example2: For x=\([0,1,2,3,4]\) and y=\([5,4,3,2,1]\), vector addition returns five fives. Extend the fixture to \(\mathrm{n}=33\) with distinct values to expose a tail just beyond a warp boundary. Test empty, singleton and a larger odd prime as well.
code:
n, stride = 19, 8
owners = [list(range(t, n, stride)) for t in range(stride)]
flat = [i for group in owners for i in group]
assert sorted(flat) == list(range(n)) and len(set(flat)) == n
assert owners[0] == [0, 8, 16]
print({"thread_0": owners[0], "all_elements_written_once": True})

tasks.question: Give the indices owned by starting thread 5 when \(\mathrm{stride}=8\) and \(\mathrm{n}=22\).
tasks.answer: The indices are 5,13,21. The next value 29 is outside the range.

tasks.question: A kernel tests `i <= n` instead of `i < n`. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: Index n lies one past the final element. A sentinel or sanitizer may catch it; lengths 1 and 33 make small useful reproducers.

tasks.question: How many blocks are required for \(\mathrm{n}=33\) with 32 threads under one-element mapping?
tasks.answer: Two blocks, with 31 inactive thread positions in the second block. Guard every output access.

tasks.question: Transfer the proof to a streaming chunk with a global offset.
tasks.answer: Compute a local bounded index first, then add a validated chunk offset. Preserve both local capacity and global destination bounds.

title: Two-dimensional indexing and image kernels
theory: `dim3`, row/column mapping, leading dimensions, rectangular shapes, pitches and boundary policy. Carefully separate logical coordinates from byte addresses.
evidence: correct non-square results, preserved padding and explicit edge behavior.
mistake: swapping grid axes only changes performance rather than which elements are touched.
mechanism: A dim3 value holds three dimensions, though an image often uses only x and y. Map x to a column and y to a row, then calculate storage using the row stride. Logical width and stored leading dimension are different quantities. The grid must cover both axes, and each thread predicates both coordinate bounds before accessing storage. This is especially important for rectangular images because square examples can conceal a swapped width and height. If an allocation uses a byte pitch, convert coordinates using that byte quantity deliberately rather than treating it as an element stride.
example1: Take a width-3, height-2 image stored as \([1,2,3,99,4,5,6,99]\) with stride four. Add ten to each real pixel. The expected storage is \([11,12,13,99,14,15,16,99]\). Both padding sentinels stay 99. Coordinate (1,2) means row one, column two, stored at index six.
example2: A 4-by-2 thread block covers a 3-by-2 image with two unused x positions, one in each row. If the image becomes 2-by-3, grid height must also grow. Checking only the flattened offset can accidentally accept a logically invalid column that lands in the next row.
code:
width, height, stride = 3, 2, 4
image = [1, 2, 3, 99, 4, 5, 6, 99]
for row in range(height):
    for col in range(width):
        image[row * stride + col] += 10
assert image == [11, 12, 13, 99, 14, 15, 16, 99]
print(image)

tasks.question: Find grid dimensions for width 17, height 9 and blocks 8-by-4.
tasks.answer: Ceiling division gives grid x=3 and y=3. Predicate each coordinate because both axes have tails.

tasks.question: Why can flattening before coordinate checks corrupt padding?
tasks.answer: An invalid x value may map inside the allocation or into another row. Storage capacity is not the same as logical image validity.

tasks.question: Specify behavior for width zero.
tasks.answer: Produce an empty logical image and skip launch; retain a clear contract for output shape and storage ownership.

tasks.question: Adapt the transform to RGB interleaved pixels.
tasks.answer: Add a channel dimension or multiply pixel offsets by three, preserving row stride and channel bounds. Document whether stride counts bytes, elements or pixels.

title: GPU memory spaces in one working program
theory: registers, local memory, global memory, shared memory, constant memory and caches; storage scope and lifetime versus hardware location. Explain that local memory is a compiler storage category, not necessarily fast on-chip storage.
evidence: a justified storage choice for each variable and a correct result across two input shapes.
mistake: every local variable stays in a register, or shared memory is shared across all blocks.
mechanism: Storage spaces describe accessibility and lifetime as well as likely performance. Global allocations can hold data used by many kernels. Shared memory belongs to a block and lasts for that block's execution. Registers hold thread-local values, but a large local array or register pressure can place values in local memory backed by device memory. Constant storage is useful for certain read-only patterns, especially broadcast-like access, but it is not an automatic speedup for arbitrary divergent addresses. A compiler resource report helps explain implementation choices; source variable scope alone does not prove where every value resides.
example1: In a three-tap filter, the input and output images live in global allocations. A thread's running sum is a scalar candidate for a register. A cooperatively loaded tile belongs in shared memory. Three common coefficients may use read-only or constant storage. These are choices to validate, not declarations that force a faster program.
example2: A per-thread temporary array with 1,024 floats needs 4,096 bytes per thread. At 128 threads that is 524,288 bytes of logical temporary data, before other resources. Calling it 'local' does not make it inexpensive. Reduce live working state or choose a different algorithm, then inspect compiler and runtime evidence.
code:
bytes_per_thread = 1024 * 4
logical_bytes_per_block = bytes_per_thread * 128
assert bytes_per_thread == 4096 and logical_bytes_per_block == 524288
placements = {"image": "global", "cooperative_tile": "shared", "sum": "thread local"}
print({"logical_temporary_bytes": logical_bytes_per_block, "storage_roles": placements})

tasks.question: Assign storage for a reused image, a block tile and a scalar sum.
tasks.answer: Global allocation for the image, shared memory for cooperating block data, and a local scalar that the compiler may keep in a register.

tasks.question: An author says a local array is guaranteed to stay in registers. Correct the claim.
tasks.answer: The compiler can place local data in device-backed local memory or spill registers. Inspect generated resource information and measured behavior.

tasks.question: Can one block read another block's ordinary shared array?
tasks.answer: No. Ordinary block shared memory has block scope. Specialized cluster mechanisms have separate feature and synchronization contracts.

tasks.question: Decide whether to use constant storage for a 64-entry lookup table.
tasks.answer: Compare whether neighboring lanes read the same entries or divergent entries, access frequency and update needs; measure against a suitable read-only/global alternative.

title: Shared memory and block synchronization
theory: cooperative loads, visibility, barriers, race conditions and divergent barrier hazards. Explain all participating threads' responsibilities before showing a shared-memory optimization. Distinguish a block barrier from a grid barrier.
evidence: correct boundary behavior and a synchronization explanation naming producer and consumer threads.
mistake: a memory fence and a barrier are interchangeable.
mechanism: Shared memory lets threads in one block communicate through a common scratch array. Communication requires ordering: a consumer must not read a location until its producer has written it. `__syncthreads()` is a block barrier with memory-ordering effects for participating threads. Put bounds predicates around loads and stores while keeping the required barrier participation uniform. Invalid tail lanes can load a neutral value and still reach the barrier. A barrier does not coordinate ordinary independent blocks, and a memory fence does not force other threads to arrive at the same program point.
example1: Four threads load \([3,6,9,12]\) into a shared tile, synchronize, then thread t reads tile[3-t]. The reversed output is \([12,9,6,3]\). Without the barrier, a consumer could read before another thread loads its value. An apparent success on one execution is not a synchronization proof.
example2: For a three-element tail in a four-thread block, lane three loads a neutral zero and still participates in the barrier. Only valid lanes store output. A conditional `if (i<n) { load; barrier; }` can violate the barrier contract when some block threads skip it.
code:
tile = [3, 6, 9, 12]
# A CPU phase boundary models the dependency, not GPU scheduling.
output = [tile[3 - lane] for lane in range(4)]
assert output == [12, 9, 6, 3]
partial = [3, 6, 9, 0]
assert sum(partial) == 18
print({"reversal": output, "neutralized_tail_sum": sum(partial)})

tasks.question: Draw the producer and consumer for reversed output index zero.
tasks.answer: Thread three produces tile\([3]\), the barrier establishes availability, and thread zero consumes it.

tasks.question: A conditional barrier hangs only on ragged input. What is the smallest repair?
tasks.answer: Move the required barrier outside the bounds condition, neutralize invalid loads and predicate only accesses that need valid indices.

tasks.question: Why does a block barrier not make a global reduction complete?
tasks.answer: Other blocks do not participate. Use separate dependent kernel stages or a qualified cooperative launch design.

tasks.question: Design a neighbor-average tile with a halo.
tasks.answer: Name owners for interior and halo loads, synchronize before consumption, define boundary values and keep output separate from input.

title: A simple matrix multiplication with a complete specification
theory: matrix dimensions, contraction, row-major offsets, accumulation type and numerical tolerance. Derive the scalar algorithm first and map one output element to a thread.
evidence: correctness across the shape suite and a transparent operation/byte estimate.
mistake: passing a square all-ones example establishes layout correctness.
mechanism: Matrix multiplication contracts a shared dimension: an m-by-k matrix A times a k-by-n matrix B produces an m-by-n matrix C. One simple CUDA thread owns one output coordinate and loops across k. Row-major A uses row*k+inner; row-major B uses inner*n+column. The output uses row*n+column. This deliberately simple kernel rereads data and serves as an understandable correctness baseline. Accumulation type and tolerance are part of its specification. Distinct entries and rectangular shapes reveal layout errors better than square all-ones inputs.
example1: Multiply \([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]\) by \([[1,2],[0,1],[2,0]]\). The output is \([[7,4],[16,13]]\). Entry (1,0) is \(4\times 1+5\times 0+6\times 2=16\). Explicitly name every dimension before translating the three scalar indices into flat offsets.
example2: Multiplying by an identity matrix preserves input, but that test alone can miss some errors. A 3-by-5 times 5-by-2 case exercises tails and asymmetric dimensions. If \(\mathrm{k}=0\), define the sum of zero products as zero and decide how the host handles the empty inputs without invalid launches.
code:
A = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
B = [[1, 2], [0, 1], [2, 0]]
C = [[sum(A[r][k] * B[k][c] for k in range(3)) for c in range(2)] for r in range(2)]
assert C == [[7, 4], [16, 13]]
print(C)

tasks.question: Compute entry (0,1) in the worked product.
tasks.answer: \(1\times 2+2\times 1+3\times 0=4\). The summation axis is k, not the output column axis.

tasks.question: An implementation swaps m and n yet passes a square test. Add a counterexample.
tasks.answer: Use unequal m and n with unique values, such as the 2-by-3 times 3-by-2 worked case plus a 3-by-5 times 5-by-2 fixture.

tasks.question: What happens when m or n is zero?
tasks.answer: The output has no elements and the host can return without launching a grid.

tasks.question: Estimate multiply-add work for \(\mathrm{m}=2\),\(\mathrm{k}=3\),\(\mathrm{n}=2\).
tasks.answer: There are 12 products and associated accumulation operations, conventionally about 24 FLOPs. State whether initialization additions are counted.

title: Tiled matrix multiplication and reuse
theory: tile loading, shared-memory reuse, synchronization between phases, tail predicates and resource costs. Derive why a tile reduces repeated global reads, while explaining that more reuse may consume more shared memory and registers.
evidence: correctness plus a measured, scoped comparison with a reasoned interpretation even if the tile loses on a small input.
mistake: shared memory automatically makes a kernel faster.
mechanism: Tiling loads small regions of A and B into shared memory and reuses each value across several output calculations. For each k-phase, threads cooperatively load both tiles, synchronize, accumulate from the tiles, then synchronize again before overwriting shared storage for the next phase. Partial tiles require zero-filled invalid positions. An early return by tail threads can break the barrier contract. Tile size trades global reuse against shared storage, registers, occupancy and unused tail work. A tiled learning kernel is a correctness and reuse experiment, not an automatic replacement for a mature GEMM library.
example1: For a 2-by-2 output tile and \(\mathrm{k}=2\), the four outputs need eight products. Loading four A values and four B values allows reuse across outputs. The naive per-output scheme conceptually reads sixteen scalar operands; the tile loads eight. Cache behavior can change actual transactions.
example2: With \(\mathrm{k}=3\) and tile width two, the second phase contains one valid inner coordinate and one zero coordinate. Neutralizing invalid A and B entries preserves the sum. Synchronize after accumulation before the next cooperative load; otherwise a fast producer can overwrite data a slower thread still reads.
code:
k, tile = 5, 2
phases = [(start, min(start + tile, k)) for start in range(0, k, tile)]
assert phases == [(0, 2), (2, 4), (4, 5)]
assert 2 * 16 * 16 * 4 == 2048
print({"phases": phases, "two_tiles_bytes": 2048})

tasks.question: Count phases for \(\mathrm{k}=5\) and tile width two.
tasks.answer: Three phases. The final phase contributes one valid inner coordinate and one neutral zero coordinate.

tasks.question: Why is returning early for an out-of-range output thread dangerous?
tasks.answer: That thread may still be required for cooperative loads and barriers. Keep all participating threads through the tile phases and predicate final stores.

tasks.question: How much shared storage do two 16-by-16 float tiles use?
tasks.answer: \(2\times 16\times 16\times 4=2,048\) bytes, before any padding or other shared objects.

tasks.question: A tiled kernel loses on a tiny matrix. Is that a bug?
tasks.answer: Not necessarily. Compare correctness first; setup, synchronization and unused lanes can outweigh reuse for small shapes.

title: Parallel reductions and the order of arithmetic
theory: tree reduction, partial sums, neutral elements, non-power-of-two lengths and numerical ordering. Use separate kernel stages for the first cross-block reduction rather than an improvised global barrier.
evidence: correct tails and a justified tolerance, with no assumption of a fixed block completion order.
mistake: floating-point addition is associative or one block can safely wait for every other block in an ordinary launch.
mechanism: A reduction combines values with an operation and identity. A tree reduces dependency depth compared with a serial chain, but it changes floating-point addition order. A block reduction usually first writes one partial per block; another launch combines those partials. This creates a real cross-block dependency without an unsafe grid-wide spin barrier. Tail threads contribute the identity, such as zero for addition. For a maximum, zero is not a neutral value if all inputs are negative. Define empty input explicitly and retain a higher-accuracy CPU oracle for floating-point work.
example1: Pad \([1,2,3,4,5]\) to \([1,2,3,4,5,0,0,0]\). A halving tree produces pairwise states \([6,2,3,4]\), then \([9,6]\), then \([15]\). Each phase needs the appropriate communication ordering. Exact integer arithmetic makes ownership mistakes visible without rounding ambiguity.
example2: For \([10^{16},1,-10^{16}]\), different valid sum trees can disagree. Compare against a compensated or higher-precision reference and report error. Do not require a GPU result to copy an arbitrary CPU association, and do not enlarge tolerance enough to hide dropped tail elements.
code:
values = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0, 0, 0]
width = len(values) // 2
trace = []
while width:
    for i in range(width):
        values[i] += values[i + width]
    trace.append(values[:width])
    width //= 2
assert trace == [[6, 2, 3, 4], [9, 6], [15]]
print(trace)

tasks.question: Choose an identity for maximum over \([-7,-3,-9]\).
tasks.answer: Negative infinity is the general floating maximum identity; zero would incorrectly dominate this entirely negative input.

tasks.question: One block waits for a counter from all other blocks. Explain the deadlock risk.
tasks.answer: Waiting blocks can occupy resources needed by unscheduled producers. Ordinary launches provide no universal simultaneous residency guarantee.

tasks.question: Define sum for zero and one element.
tasks.answer: The empty sum is zero; the singleton sum equals that element. Avoid invalid zero-block launches.

tasks.question: Transfer reduction to mean.
tasks.answer: Reduce both sum and count, then divide only when count is nonzero; define the empty mean policy explicitly.

title: Scans and stream compaction
theory: inclusive versus exclusive prefix sums, local scan and block offsets, work-efficient design, stable compaction and allocation of output positions. Explain the link between scan and parallel data structure construction.
evidence: exact output counts and element order for empty, all-match and no-match cases.
mistake: a parallel sum is enough to recover every element's output position.
mechanism: An exclusive scan gives each item the reduction of preceding items; an inclusive scan includes the item itself. For stable compaction, map the selection predicate to zeros and ones, scan those flags, then let selected input i write to its exclusive prefix position. Stability means selected elements keep their relative order. Multiple blocks require scanning block totals and adding offsets in another stage. A total count says how much output is needed but does not assign every destination. Separate input and output or prove that aliasing cannot overwrite unread values.
example1: For values \([8,3,6,1,4]\), select even values. Flags are \([1,0,1,0,1]\), exclusive positions are \([0,1,1,2,2]\), and selected writes produce \([8,6,4]\). Nonselected elements have positions too, but they do not write.
example2: For flags \([0,0,0]\), the exclusive scan is \([0,0,0]\) and count is zero. For \([1,1,1]\), positions are \([0,1,2]\) and count is three. These cases catch allocating from the final exclusive prefix alone without adding the final flag.
code:
values = [8, 3, 6, 1, 4]
flags = [int(v % 2 == 0) for v in values]
positions, count = [], 0
for flag in flags:
    positions.append(count)
    count += flag
out = [None] * count
for v, flag, position in zip(values, flags, positions):
    if flag:
        out[position] = v
assert out == [8, 6, 4] and positions == [0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
print({"flags": flags, "positions": positions, "compacted": out})

tasks.question: Compact \([5,2,7,8]\) for values greater than four.
tasks.answer: Flags \([1,0,1,1]\), positions \([0,1,1,2]\), output \([5,7,8]\). The preserved order is part of the contract.

tasks.question: Why is the last exclusive prefix insufficient for count?
tasks.answer: It excludes the last element. Count equals final prefix plus final flag for nonempty input.

tasks.question: What are scan and compact outputs for empty input?
tasks.answer: Both are empty and count is zero; no last-element access is valid.

tasks.question: Use scan to build ragged row offsets from lengths \([2,0,3]\).
tasks.answer: Exclusive offsets are \([0,2,2]\); append total five to obtain \([0,2,2,5]\), the row-boundary representation.

title: Histograms, atomics and contention
theory: conflicting writes, atomic updates, collision probability and block privatization. Separate atomicity from ordering and discuss why a skewed input is an essential performance test.
evidence: exact counts and a contention-based explanation of two timing regimes.
mistake: an atomic operation is either always fast or always slow, independent of access pattern.
mechanism: A histogram counts values into bins. Several threads can increment the same bin, so ordinary read-modify-write operations can lose updates. An atomic addition makes that individual update indivisible at its supported scope. It does not make an entire multi-step algorithm atomic or publish unrelated data automatically. A block-private histogram can reduce global contention by combining local counts before a global merge. It also costs shared memory and initialization work. Distribution matters: uniformly spread samples and one hot bin exercise very different contention patterns even with identical input size.
example1: Values \([0,2,2,1,2,0]\) with three bins produce \([2,1,3]\). The sum of bins is six. Two workers both reading an old count of zero and then each writing one lose a count; correct atomic accumulation produces two.
example2: Split the values into two groups of three. Their private histograms are \([1,0,2]\) and \([1,1,1]\); merging gives \([2,1,3]\). This explains the algorithm without promising the private version is faster. For small inputs, initialization and merging may cost more than direct atomic updates.
code:
values = [0, 2, 2, 1, 2, 0]


def histogram(items):
    bins = [0, 0, 0]
    for value in items:
        assert 0 <= value < len(bins)
        bins[value] += 1
    return bins


parts = [histogram(values[:3]), histogram(values[3:])]
merged = [sum(pair) for pair in zip(*parts)]
assert merged == [2, 1, 3] and sum(merged) == len(values)
print({"partials": parts, "merged": merged})

tasks.question: Build a four-bin histogram of \([3,3,0,1,3]\).
tasks.answer: \([1,1,0,3]\), with total five. Include the empty bin in validation.

tasks.question: The input contains category -1. Define a safe contract.
tasks.answer: Reject it before indexing or explicitly count it in an overflow category. Never let it address memory before the bins.

tasks.question: What fixture maximizes simple same-bin contention?
tasks.answer: Repeating one category for every element; compare with a spread distribution under the same count and bin size.

tasks.question: Transfer histograms to quantized floating measurements.
tasks.answer: Specify bin edges, inclusivity, out-of-range and NaN policies before mapping values to integer bins.

title: Stencils and boundary conditions
theory: neighborhood reuse, halo cells, read/write separation, time steps and physical versus computational boundaries. Define clamp, periodic and fixed-value policies before coding.
evidence: correct interior and boundary values plus a conserved or monotonic quantity appropriate to the chosen model.
mistake: a visually plausible image proves the indexing and update ordering are correct.
mechanism: A stencil computes each output from a neighborhood of input values. The boundary policy is part of the mathematics: clamped, periodic and fixed-zero boundaries describe different problems. Use separate input and output buffers for a time step so one update cannot change a neighbor's inputs halfway through the step. A tiled implementation loads a halo around its interior region because edge outputs need values from neighboring tiles. A barrier only protects data loaded by the same cooperating group; it does not legalize global in-place updates across independently scheduled blocks.
example1: For \([2,4,8]\) with a three-point mean and fixed-zero outside values, one step gives \([2,\frac{14}{3},4]\). With clamped boundaries it gives \([\frac{8}{3},\frac{14}{3},\frac{20}{3}]\). Both are valid calculations, but they answer different questions. A reference must match the chosen policy.
example2: An in-place left-to-right update reads newly computed values for later neighbors, creating a directional bias. Two-buffer updates read only the original row and swap roles after completion. For multiple GPU steps, preserve the dependency between launches or streams before swapping logical roles.
code:
values = [2.0, 4.0, 8.0]


def at(i):
    return values[i] if 0 <= i < len(values) else 0.0


out = [(at(i - 1) + at(i) + at(i + 1)) / 3 for i in range(len(values))]
assert out == [2.0, 14 / 3, 4.0]
assert values == [2.0, 4.0, 8.0]
print({"fixed_zero_mean": out, "original_preserved": values})

tasks.question: Compute the periodic neighbor mean for \([2,4,8]\).
tasks.answer: Every three-element neighborhood contains all three values, so each output is \(\frac{14}{3}\).

tasks.question: An image looks smooth but differs near the edge. Investigate what first?
tasks.answer: Compare the documented boundary policy, halo loading and row stride before changing the smoothing formula or tolerance.

tasks.question: What is a radius-one fixed-zero stencil of singleton \([6]\)?
tasks.answer: (\(0+6+0\))/\(3=2\) under the stated mean. A clamped rule instead returns six.

tasks.question: Transfer the method to diffusion time stepping.
tasks.answer: Define timestep and stability assumptions, separate old/new fields, exchange halos where needed and check an appropriate conservation or monotonicity property.

title: First capstone: a reliable GPU data pipeline
theory: composition of validated kernels, data ownership across stages, bounded input contracts and meaningful application timing.
evidence: a specification, CPU oracle, adversarial fixtures, checked error paths, actual GPU output and honest end-to-end report.
mistake: individual correct kernels necessarily compose correctly when buffers, shapes or ownership differ.
mechanism: A pipeline is more than a list of correct kernels. Each stage has a shape, ownership and validity contract that must match its consumer. Filtering changes count; normalization changes numeric range; histogramming assumes valid bins. Keep the count with the output buffer, and do not pass allocation capacity as the number of valid elements. First build a tiny CPU oracle, then introduce one GPU stage at a time. A useful capstone report includes cases where a CPU is preferable, because proving that a GPU exists is different from proving it helps the application.
example1: A synthetic event pipeline keeps nonnegative values from \([-2,1,3,-1,2]\), producing \([1,3,2]\). It computes count three, sum six and mean two. A histogram over bins 0 through 3 gives \([0,1,1,1]\). This ties compaction output count to every downstream stage.
example2: An empty selection from \([-4,-1]\) has count zero and sum zero, but no defined ordinary arithmetic mean. Return a named empty-result status or optional mean rather than dividing by zero. The histogram remains four zeros under this contract.
code:
values = [-2, 1, 3, -1, 2]
selected = [v for v in values if v >= 0]
bins = [selected.count(i) for i in range(4)]
assert selected == [1, 3, 2] and bins == [0, 1, 1, 1]
result = {"count": len(selected), "sum": sum(selected), "mean": sum(selected) / len(selected)}
assert result == {"count": 3, "sum": 6, "mean": 2.0}
print(result, bins)

tasks.question: Specify the pipeline output for \([0,0,3]\).
tasks.answer: Count three, sum three, mean one and histogram \([2,0,0,1]\) under four bins.

tasks.question: A downstream kernel consumes capacity ten after only three items were selected. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: Capacity is storage extent, not valid count. Carry the selected count explicitly and bound downstream reads by it.

tasks.question: Add a value 7 when only bins 0 through 3 are supported.
tasks.answer: Reject or explicitly extend the declared bin policy. Do not silently clamp unless clamping is part of the specification.

tasks.question: Define a fair end-to-end comparison.
tasks.answer: Use identical selection, aggregation and result semantics; include required transfers and allocation or document reused state, retain samples and compare numerical outputs first.

title: A disciplined CUDA error taxonomy
theory: compilation, linking, loading, invalid launch, allocation, asynchronous execution and application-validation failures. Teach how earlier asynchronous errors can be observed by later API calls, and why a clean status at one point is not whole-program proof.
evidence: a useful bug report that includes the smallest reproducer and the responsible phase.
mistake: every error is fixed by reinstalling CUDA or rebuilding every image.
mechanism: Debugging starts by placing a failure in its phase. A source error prevents compilation; a missing symbol prevents linking; incompatible device code can prevent loading; invalid launch parameters can reject submission; an illegal access can fail asynchronous execution; and a completed kernel can still calculate the wrong answer. Later CUDA calls may surface an earlier asynchronous failure, so the line reporting an error is not always the line that caused it. Use checked phase boundaries in a debug configuration and retain the earliest meaningful diagnostic. Avoid reinstalling tools before a small reproducer isolates the responsible layer.
example1: A misspelled identifier in main.cu produces a compiler error before any device work. Fixing bounds checks cannot help until the file compiles. Record the diagnostic with source line and build command, and rerun the smallest compilation step.
example2: A launch is accepted but a checked synchronization reports an illegal memory access. Now examine ownership and bounds near that launch. If synchronization succeeds and one output is wrong, inspect arithmetic, layout or uninitialized data instead. These outcomes require different next experiments.
code:
failures = {
    "unknown identifier": "compile",
    "undefined reference": "link",
    "illegal access at completion": "execute",
    "wrong sum": "validate",
}
assert failures["wrong sum"] == "validate"
assert failures["unknown identifier"] != failures["illegal access at completion"]
print(failures)

tasks.question: Classify an undefined reference to a host helper.
tasks.answer: Host linking failed; provide the helper definition or link the correct object/library before investigating GPU execution.

tasks.question: Why add synchronization after each stage only during localization?
tasks.answer: It narrows which launch caused an asynchronous error, but changes scheduling and performance. Remove unnecessary synchronization after the dependency bug is repaired.

tasks.question: What does a no-device status mean for a numerical test?
tasks.answer: The required runtime is unavailable; the numerical test did not execute and must not pass.

tasks.question: Write a minimal bug report for a shape-dependent wrong answer.
tasks.answer: Include source revision, exact shape/dtype/data generator, expected and observed values, launch geometry, device/software identity and smallest failing index.

expected_output: {'unknown identifier': 'compile', 'undefined reference': 'link', 'illegal access at completion': 'execute', 'wrong sum': 'validate'}

title: Compute Sanitizer as evidence, with its limits
theory: distinguish memory-access, shared-memory hazard, initialization and synchronization checks. Explain overhead, tool-specific scope and meaningful nonzero exit policy. Sanitizer success is one check, not a proof of all race freedom or mathematical correctness.
evidence: the broken fixture produces the intended diagnostic, the repair passes that check and numerical tests still pass.
mistake: a sanitizer pass proves speed, all global ordering, or correctness for every input. .
mechanism: Compute Sanitizer provides several checks with different scopes. Memcheck investigates invalid and misaligned memory accesses; racecheck investigates shared-memory hazards; initcheck investigates uninitialized global-memory reads; synccheck investigates invalid synchronization use. Their observations complement mathematical tests. Instrumentation can be expensive and can change timing, so sanitizer runs are not performance samples. An automated command should select a nonzero error-exitcode, because a tool diagnostic must make the check fail even if the application itself returns success. Never conclude that one clean run proves race freedom for every input or validates unsupported global protocols.
example1: For an array of four elements, valid indices are 0 through 3. A kernel that accesses index four has an off-by-one defect even if the returned allocation happens to contain readable bytes nearby. Memcheck is an appropriate additional diagnostic, while a CPU bounds model pinpoints the invalid logical access without a GPU.
example2: A consumer reads shared tile\([2]\) before its producer writes. Racecheck can add evidence about that hazard. Replacing the missing barrier with a host sleep does not establish an ordering relationship between those threads. Repair the dependency and still validate returned numerical values.
code:
n = 4
indices = list(range(5))
invalid = [i for i in indices if not 0 <= i < n]
assert invalid == [4]
checker = {
    "out_of_bounds": "memcheck",
    "shared_hazard": "racecheck",
    "uninitialized": "initcheck",
    "invalid_barrier": "synccheck",
}
print({"CPU_bounds_audit": invalid, "tool_selection": checker})

tasks.question: Choose a checker for an uninitialized global output read.
tasks.answer: Initcheck addresses that class; retain ordinary result checks because initialization alone does not prove the formula is correct.

tasks.question: Why should the command set --error-exitcode 99?
tasks.answer: It makes detected tool errors visible to automation through a nonzero status rather than relying on manual log inspection.

tasks.question: Does a passing check at \(\mathrm{n}=32\) establish \(\mathrm{n}=33\) safety?
tasks.answer: No. A ragged tail changes participating accesses and possibly synchronization. Include both sizes and additional relevant boundaries.

tasks.question: Design an acceptance sequence after a shared-memory repair.
tasks.answer: Confirm the intended failing fixture diagnoses the old problem, run the corrected checker, validate normal/tail outputs and benchmark separately without instrumentation.

title: Race reasoning, masks and warp cooperation
theory: warp participation, active masks, collective operations, shuffle exchanges and explicit synchronization. Independent thread scheduling means old implicit lockstep assumptions are unsafe as a general correctness argument.
evidence: correct results across all tail sizes and a written participation invariant.
mistake: a full bit mask is automatically correct for a collective executed by only some lanes.
mechanism: Warp collectives require agreement about participating lanes. A mask names lanes expected to take part in a synchronized intrinsic, and source lanes used by a shuffle must actually participate. Independent thread scheduling means a convenient source ordering is not a general synchronization guarantee. Partial warps and divergent predicates need explicit reasoning. One safe educational reduction pattern has all lanes in a full warp participate, assigns zero to invalid data lanes, and then uses a full mask. A genuinely partial group needs a suitable mask and algorithm, not the same mask pasted everywhere.
example1: Eight selected lanes among a full 32-thread warp contribute values 1 through 8; other lanes contribute zero. All 32 lanes execute the collective, giving sum 36. This is different from launching only eight threads and pretending the absent 24 lanes participate.
example2: A ballot for predicates true at lanes 0,2 and 5 has bit mask 37: binary positions contribute \(1+4+32\). Population count is three. Reading a shuffled value from lane seven is not justified if lane seven is outside the participating group.
code:
mask = sum(1 << lane for lane in (0, 2, 5))
assert mask == 37 and mask.bit_count() == 3
contributions = list(range(1, 9)) + [0] * 24
assert sum(contributions) == 36
print({"ballot_mask": mask, "count": mask.bit_count(), "sum": sum(contributions)})

tasks.question: Construct a ballot mask for lanes 1,3 and 4.
tasks.answer: The bits contribute \(2+8+16=26\); the selected-lane count is three.

tasks.question: A shuffle uses a full mask inside a branch reached by half the warp. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: The mask names lanes that do not execute the collective. Reorganize participation or use a correctly defined group and algorithm.

tasks.question: What happens for no selected values in a full participating warp?
tasks.answer: Every data contribution is zero and the reduction is zero; participation and data selection are different concepts.

tasks.question: Transfer warp cooperation to segmented data.
tasks.answer: Define membership separately for each segment, ensure each collective's source/destination lanes belong to the group and test segments crossing warp boundaries.

title: Memory ordering and atomic scope
theory: atomicity, visibility, ordering, acquire/release, memory fences and thread/block/device/system scope. Teach happens-before diagrams and avoid presenting spin-wait patterns as a safe general grid barrier.
evidence: the learner can explain what each synchronization operation establishes and what it does not.
mistake: incrementing an atomic flag automatically publishes all other writes to every possible observer.
mechanism: Atomicity means one operation is indivisible with respect to competing operations at its scope. Ordering specifies how memory operations relate; visibility concerns which observer can see writes. Publishing a payload through a flag requires a protocol that orders the payload write before a release operation and the consumer's payload read after an appropriate acquire. Both sides must use compatible synchronization and scope. A relaxed atomic counter can correctly count events without publishing unrelated payloads. A fence orders operations but does not force another block to run, so it cannot repair a residency deadlock in an improvised global barrier.
example1: A producer writes payload 42, then releases a ready flag. A consumer acquires that publication before reading the payload. The happens-before chain connects payload write to payload read. This is a conceptual protocol; an actual CUDA implementation must use supported atomic types, scope and participating execution conditions.
